articles.title: Self-testing in Fermionic Networks
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-testing certifies quantum states and measurements from observed correlations alone, without assumptions on the inner workings of the devices. Its standard formulation, however, models the devices as manipulating qudits, of arbitrary or even infinite dimension. Yet febits, information encoded in the presence or absence of a fermion in a mode, can produce correlations in quantum networks that no qudit model reproduces under the same locality constraints. We first show that the modeling choice in terms of qudits or febits matters for self-testing: some correlations that self-test a unique qudit strategy admit two fermionic realizations inequivalent under local parity-preserving isometries. We then develop a fermionic self-testing framework and show that the correlations of a three-party rewiring network single out febit states and measurements up to such isometries, providing the first genuine fermionic self-test.

articles.title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

articles.title: Agentic MLIR-to-QIR Translation with Dual-Backend Testing: A Hybrid Deterministic and LLM Approach
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25106v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum frameworks each define their own Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect, so porting a circuit to a Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR) runtime needs a hand-written pass per dialect. Our translator selects among three paths: a deterministic compiler path for known grammars (Catalyst and Quake), a large language model (LLM) agentic path for unseen dialects, and a repair path invoked when deterministic output fails testing. A dual-backend pipeline executes the source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators, comparing output distributions by total variation distance (TVD). For smaller open-weight models we replace retrieval-augmented generation with inline context engineering and add a guardrail-assembler that rebuilds valid QIR from incomplete output. Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 1-100 qubits, the deterministic path is gate-exact on all 70 circuit-dialect pairs, averaging above 95% TVD similarity (1-TVD). On an unseen fault-tolerant (FTQC) dialect, four of six models produce valid logical-level QIR on the first iteration.

articles.title: Generalizing and Combining Check Constructions: Design-Space Exploration for Fault-Tolerant Quantum State Preparation
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical states prepared such that single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection achieves this with added checks that detect dangerous faults and discard the run. How the checks are measured sets the depth and operation count of the circuit, and the best trade-off depends on the hardware. Existing automated methods, however, each use one check construction and yield fixed trade-offs. We first introduce Block Checks, in which several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which places them and existing constructions in a single design space. Second, to explore that space, we propose a Pareto tree search that adds checks and auxiliary blocks, merges auxiliaries, and edits the circuit. On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation--depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) at https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/qecc, and all circuits are available in the QECirc library at https://qecirc.com.

articles.title: A Quantum Continuous Wavelet Transform
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a quantum continuous wavelet transform (QCWT) on a finite scale--translation grid whose scales may be non-dyadic. A quantum Fourier transform places the amplitude-encoded signal in the frequency basis, the scale-dependent multiplier is block-encoded with one flag qubit, and an inverse Fourier transform returns the complex, quadrature-weighted CWT coefficients in the success branch. For heralded circuits that act once on one copy of the input with an input-independent output factor, we bound the success probability and attain the bound by a frequency-conditioned scale preparation. When the scale prior is prepared independently of frequency, normalizing the multiplier separately at each scale is optimal and raises the success probability by factors of 4.9 and 14.6 in our examples; on logarithmic grids this architecture loses, relative to the bound, a factor of about the admissibility constant over the squared spectral peak times the logarithmic scale range. We give a fixed-point resource estimate for a reversible Mexican-hat multiplier, the multinomial law of scale--translation measurements, and Hadamard tests for complex coefficients. We show that a Fourier-basis measurement of the input, followed by classical randomization, reproduces the flag and scale outcomes of every such heralded circuit exactly, so it is at least as informative for global scale energies; a simulation study of Hurst exponent estimation agrees. What the QCWT adds is the joint scale--translation law: two chirps with identical Fourier-basis and

articles.title: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times in Quantum Phase Estimation
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning a Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation that produces phase distributions with low Shannon entropy circumvents the fundamental limit of digitization error of phase, independent of the number of phase qubits of accuracy. By introducing an optimization loop to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalues produced by a QPE quantum circuit, minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy is greatly improved, which we show numerically on quantum magnet models. This technique works because standard QPE has a natural correspondence between entropy of the phase distribution and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase. This introduces for the first time a type of parameter learning to QPE, which makes near term practicality of QPE for fundamental sciences more feasible by using shorter depth QPE circuits.

articles.title: Characterizing a neutral atom quantum simulator accessible in cloud
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulators have become a reality in recent years, with several platforms now remotely accessible through the cloud. These systems give researchers the opportunity to run quantum programs without requiring either a dedicated laboratory or extensive experimental expertise, and, in several cases, they have already enabled the execution of relevant protocols with remarkable results. However, despite the impressive progress in the performance of these machines, they still suffer from various noise sources, some of which are not always completely clear to the end user, which limits their applicability to tasks that are sufficiently robust against noise of various kinds. In this work, we investigate the behavior of Fresnel, a remotely accessible neutral-atom analog quantum simulator provided by Pasqal. We design and perform a series of experiments probing the machine's response to various pulse sequences and experimental settings, and identify the main noise sources affecting its dynamics. Based on these data, we construct an effective model of the system's noisy evolution and use numerical optimization to infer the noise strengths. The resulting model accurately reproduces the simulator's dynamics, showing how effective noise models can be built for cloud-based quantum resources.

articles.title: Accelerating Diffusion Maps on a Quantum Computer: Spectral Filtering and Galerkin PDE Solvers
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion maps generalize principal component analysis (PCA) to nonlinear manifolds, enabling spectral dimensionality reduction, geometric data analysis, and elliptic PDE approximation on point clouds. For large datasets of size $N$, however, classical matrix operations incur prohibitive $\operatorname{poly}(N)$ scaling, even when extracting low-dimensional spectral features or targeted scalar observables. We introduce a quantum algorithmic framework that bypasses explicit graph-Laplacian assembly by exploiting the symmetric factorization $G = A^T A$ directly at the block-encoding level. Combining Gaussian moment dilation, Laplace-weighted linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), we implement spectral filters of $A$ to estimate heat-semigroup overlaps, regularized inverse queries, and energy responses, as well as to prepare spectral Galerkin solution states. A common-state construction further allows the block-encoding queries to be used across multiple scalar observables. Under polylogarithmic-cost block-encoding access to $A$ and state-preparation oracles, our heat-overlap algorithm achieves $O(\operatorname{polylog} N)$ gate complexity at fixed normalized precision, confidence, and spectral scale. Ideal statevector simulations validate our discrete circuit constructions, while a matched approximate-counting benchmark demonstrates the quadratic precision advantage of coherent amplitude estimation for energy readout.

articles.title: Analytic and Numerical Investigation of a Proposed Non-linear Extension of Quantum Mechanics
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, additional properties of a previously introduced non-linear extension of quantum mechanics are investigated. Analytically, we uncover a limit in which the model reduces to ordinary linear quantum mechanics. We also perform a perturbation analysis about an exact solution studied in earlier work. The equations represent a system that is subject to a periodic driver, and we use Floquet theory to help determine its properties. Numerically, we compare the exact solution to the analytic approximation, and we exhibit several examples of how the non-linear effects influence particle trajectories, with particular emphasis on trajectories near the linear limit.

articles.title: Tunable source of entangled microwaves by nonlinear scattering of magnons
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a route to prepare entangled states of microwaves propagating in spatially separated transmission lines using the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of ferromagnetic spin waves (magnons). We first show that a driven magnon mode can produce entangled magnon pairs at low temperatures by spontaneous parametric down-conversion enabled by three-magnon processes. The anisotropic magnon properties in thin films result in strict phase-matching conditions which allow only a well-defined pair of magnon modes to be amplified. This mode selectivity allows to out-couple each amplified mode to an independent microwave transmission line, producing non-degenerate propagating microwave entanglement with current experimental parameters. In addition, we prove that the frequency difference between the two entangled microwaves can be dynamically tuned across a few-GHz range by changing the orientation of a bias magnetic field. Our figures of merit - .g., the amount of microwave entanglement - can be largely improved by optimizing material and geometry. Our work establishes that quantum states of propagating magnons can be created by their nonlinear dynamics alone, and opens a pathway toward integrating magnons in hybrid quantum platforms.

articles.title: Certified Separation Between Coherent and Adaptive Temporal Processing of Quantum-Error-Correction Readout
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Repeated quantum-error-correction readout is normally converted into a classical time series: each syndrome pulse is measured on arrival and only the resulting classical record is retained. Nonorthogonal readout signals raise the question of whether preserving quantum information between rounds can improve the final recovery decision. We formulate this comparison as a loss-weighted state-discrimination problem. For an idealized two-round benchmark with quadrature phase-shift-keying (QPSK) signals, a receiver with a seven-dimensional persistent register has certified recovery-decision error below $24.2100\%$, whereas every separate adaptive receiver has error above $25.1431\%$. The certified separation is at least $0.933$ percentage points. The loss counts incorrect final error-mask decisions in the benchmark. In the strict architecture, where the counted register is the entire persistent state, four dimensions are necessary and sufficient to outperform the adaptive class. Certified separations also occur at three and four rounds with register dimensions $8$ and $36$, compared with $16$ and $64$ for full-prefix storage. We relate memory dimension to the structure of the temporal measurement, give a sufficient memory bound for collective measurements, and quantify robustness to register dephasing and accumulated channel error.

articles.title: Resilience of emergent Hamiltonian quantum memories in the presence of noise
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emergent Hamiltonians can freeze an entangled state prepared through coherent evolution, since that state is an eigenstate of the Hamiltonian under which it is then stored. We show that the freedom left in this construction allows the storage spectrum to be adapted to a noisy environment without changing the stored state. For a product of Bell pairs prepared from a density wave in an engineered chain, a selection rule prevents local density noise from connecting the target to any of its degenerate partners, so that rescaling the storage Hamiltonian by a factor $\alpha$ moves every transition this noise drives. Under $1/f$ noise, the storage time then grows in proportion to $\alpha$, a result we confirm by evolving the memory under explicit classical $1/f$ fields, whereas for an Ohmic bath the most favorable scale depends on its cutoff. Fermionic loss, treated as a solvable model, includes a transition that rescaling leaves at zero frequency, and an energy shift $\mu$ per particle moves it away from zero, with an exact orbital solution giving the resulting lifetimes. Finally, among number-conserving quadratic reference Hamiltonians, $\alpha$ and $\mu$ are the only controls that keep the storage Hamiltonian nearest neighbor at every time along the preparation, so that the protocol combines local freezing with control over the storage spectrum.

articles.title: Quantum dynamical transitions when the corresponding classical phase space has a separatrix: extension of the QKNH theorem beyond double wells
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.25299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In classical Hamiltonian systems with a slowly time-dependent parameter, adiabaticity breaks down at a separatrix, leading to probabilistic post-adiabatic transitions between different phase-space regions described by the Kruskal-Neishtadt-Henrard (KNH) theorem. Quantum mechanically, dynamical tunneling allows adiabaticity to persist where it breaks down classically, making the quantum-classical correspondence for separatrix crossing non-trivial. We recently established a quantum version of the KNH theorem (QKNH) by introducing the concept of a sweep-rate-dependent quantum separatrix in the instantaneous energy spectrum of the time-dependent system. The QKNH theorem relates the splitting of a quantum ensemble between the outgoing dynamical sectors at the quantum separatrix to their relative growth rates, and thus provides a quantum analog of the classical KNH rule. Here, we demonstrate that these findings are not restricted to double-well systems with tunneling through a potential barrier. We investigate a slowly driven quantum pendulum, in which the avoided crossings arise from above-barrier reflection. The resulting Landau-Zener probabilities have the same local lattice form as in the double-well problem, allowing the application of the QKNH theorem.

articles.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
articles.summary: Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity—brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay—in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal–neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

articles.title: A kinetic error filtering mechanism for enzyme-free copying of nucleic acid sequences
articles.summary: Accurate copying of nucleic acid sequences is essential for self-replicating systems. Modern cells achieve error ratios as low as 10−9 with sophisticated enzymes capable of kinetic proofreading. In contrast, experiments probing enzyme-free copying of RNA and DNA as potential prebiotic replication processes find error ratios on the order of 10%. Given this low intrinsic copying fidelity, plausible scenarios for the spontaneous emergence of molecular evolution require an accuracy-enhancing mechanism. Here, we study a 'kinetic error filtering' scenario that dramatically boosts the likelihood of producing exact copies of nucleic acid sequences. The mechanism exploits the observation that initial errors in template-directed polymerization of both DNA and RNA are likely to trigger a cascade of consecutive errors and significantly stall downstream extension. We incorporate these characteristics into a mathematical model with experimentally estimated parameters, and leverage this model to probe to what extent accurate and faulty polymerization products can be kinetically discriminated. Limiting the time window for polymerization prevents completion of erroneous strands, resulting in a pool in which full-length products show an enhanced accuracy. This comes at the price of a concomitant reduction in yield. However, the yield rate and the fidelity can be simultaneously increased by kinetic error filtering, if the templates are not too long. articles.title: Integrating distributed lag non-linear models and deep learning reveals meteorological drivers of influenza A and B positivity in a 6-year subtropical surveillance study
articles.summary: Subtropical influenza forecasting is complicated by non-linear meteorological dynamics and surveillance bias stemming from pandemic-era testing fluctuations. Existing approaches either characterize lagged environmental associations without forecasting capacity or apply deep learning without epidemiological interpretability. We analyzed multisite influenza surveillance data from Putian, southeastern China (2018–2023); test positivity was the primary outcome to mitigate testing-related bias. Distributed lag nonlinear models estimated type-specific associations between eight meteorological variables and positivity over a 15-day lag window. A Bayesian-optimized long short-term memory (LSTM) network incorporating meteorological, autoregressive, and socio-behavioral covariates was benchmarked against covariate-matched multivariate autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) models. For influenza A, the temperature-associated relative risk (RR) peaked at 15°C (3.01; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.03–8.78), and positivity was associated with narrow diurnal temperature ranges. Influenza B positivity was associated with colder conditions (8°C; RR = 26.12, 95% CI: 7.79–87.61), higher humidity (91%; RR = 1.52, 95% CI: 1.00–2.29), and lower solar radiation. The LSTM had lower mean absolute error for influenza A (0.009 vs 0.136 for ARIMA and 0.138 for XGBoost) and B (0.002 vs 0.049 and 0.070); symmetric mean absolute percentage error was 0.521 vs 1.212 and 1.081 for A and 0.484 vs 0.810 and 0.737 for B. Covariate ablation and Shapley additive

articles.title: Blood-derived dietary protein promotes sleep in the mosquito Aedes aegypti
articles.summary: Sleep is a ubiquitous, yet highly variable, behavior across species. The duration and timing of sleep are influenced by ecological demands and dietary context. In the mosquito Aedes aegypti, a blood-feeding insect with specialized nutritional requirements, the relationship between feeding and sleep remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how blood-derived dietary protein influences sleep regulation. Using postural analysis, videography, and arousal-threshold assays, we established that immobility bouts of ≥10 min reliably define sleep in A. aegypti. Mosquitoes lacking the circadian clock gene cycle still maintained daily sleep rhythms but exhibited reduced sleep duration and heightened overall activity. Infrared activity monitoring revealed that blood-fed females showed a marked increase in sleep beginning immediately after feeding and persisting for several days, accompanied by reduced locomotor activity. Notably, this sleep elevation lasted well beyond the cessation of previously reported host-seeking phases, raising the possibility of distinct phases of opportunistic vs. targeted host pursuit. To determine the dietary basis of this effect, we tested mosquitoes fed a bovine serum albumin (BSA)-based diet. BSA feeding alone was sufficient to mimic the sleep-promoting and activity-reducing effects of blood, suggesting dietary protein is a major nutritional regulator. Moreover, RNAi-mediated knockdown of the leucokinin receptor (Lkr), which has previously been associated with fluid homeostasis and feeding behavior, resulted in enhanced sl

articles.title: Calibrated analysis framework for nanopore direct RNA sequencing uncovers cell-specific m⁶A proportions at conserved sites
articles.summary: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) coupled with Dorado modification-aware base calling enables mapping of epitranscriptomic modifications including N<sup>6</sup>-methyladenosine (m<sup>6</sup>A) at the level of individual RNAs. However, the sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility of this method remain unclear and have only recently begun to be addressed through systematic benchmarking studies. Here, we aimed to establish a best-practice workflow for DRS-based epitranscriptomic analyses. Specifically, we evaluated multiple Dorado versions and models using RNA isolated from primary cells and unmodified in vitro transcribed RNAs. We further utilized an m<sup>6</sup>A methyltransferase inhibitor as a specificity control. We established that stringent filtering is necessary to reduce the contribution of background and found that Dorado predictions captured an increasing proportion of GLORI sites detected at high m<sup>6</sup>A/A proportions. Further, by applying DRS to a human primary fibroblast and a HD10.6 neuron dataset, we detected differences in the predicted m<sup>6</sup>A/A proportions at conserved sites between these datasets. Our study thus presents the first systematic comparison of Dorado and GLORI from the same input RNA and expands characterization of the m<sup>6</sup>A epitranscriptome to fibroblasts and neurons.

articles.title: Cognitive control networks in human and macaque
articles.summary: A much-replicated finding in human brain imaging is a distributed ‘multiple-demand’ or MD system, increasing in activity for many kinds of cognitive demand, and centrally involved in cognitive control. MD regions are proposed to encode a distributed mental model of critical task events, bound together in the roles and relationships needed to direct action selection. Though previous data hint at a corresponding network in the macaque, there has been no direct comparison to human data. Here we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to measure whole-brain activation in a multi-step saccadic maze task, compared to a control requiring similar moves but without goal-based decisions. Human data were a close match to the canonical MD network, extended to include adjacent regions, and in particular much of the canonical dorsal attention network. Data from two monkeys suggested correspondences in dorsomedial frontal, insula/orbitofrontal, and posterior temporal cortex. In lateral frontal cortex, there was just a single, largely dorsal activation patch, in contrast to multiple distinct human patches. In one animal, as in humans, there was accompanying activation of dorsal and medial parietal cortex. In macaques, as in humans, together with previous data, our findings suggest an extended and strongly interconnected brain network recruited by increased cognitive challenge.

articles.summary: Ill mental health is a big factor in holding back young people from joining the job market. Katie Pybus and Melanie Chan-Sing Coates look at the Milburn Report’s provisions for tackling mental health barriers to work and argue that while part of its approach is admirably supportive, another part seems needlessly punitive and counterproductive. The … Continued The post The mental health tension at the heart of the Milburn Report first appeared on LSE British Politics .

articles.title: Friendship across class is about more than social mobility
articles.summary: Social mobility is supposed to be the social benefit of friendships across class, according to some economists. But Sam Friedman and Rose Butler argue that the lack of reciprocity in such friendships often sabotages them. Only under the practice of “class diplomacy” can such friendships survive, and help not just with social mobility, but with … Continued The post Friendship across class is about more than social mobility first appeared on LSE British Politics .

articles.title: The Bapat-Sunder eigenvalue conjecture fails over the reals
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 1986 Bapat and Sunder asked whether $\operatorname{per}(A)$ is the largest eigenvalue of $F_A=[a_{i,j}\operatorname{per}(A(i,j))]$ for every positive semidefinite Hermitian $A$, where $A(i,j)$ deletes row $i$ and column $j$. Drury disproved this over the complex field in 2018 and conjectured that the property holds for real positive semidefinite matrices. We disprove Drury's conjecture with a rank-$4$, $32\times32$ integer Gram matrix and an integer vector whose Rayleigh quotient exceeds $\operatorname{per}(A)$; verification uses integer arithmetic. Together, the two counterexamples resolve the Bapat-Sunder eigenvalue conjecture negatively over both fields. Counterexamples exist of every order $n\ge32$. As an application to quantum optics, the violation yields a $36$-mode orthogonal interferometer and a direction of relative arrival-time delays among $32$ photons with identical-variance Gaussian wave packets along which every sufficiently small nonzero delay increases the probability that all photons are detected within four designated output modes.

articles.title: Scrambling leads to entanglement cost in NLQC
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a non-local quantum computation (NLQC), shared entanglement along with a single simultaneous round of quantum communication is used to implement a joint channel. NLQC has many applications, most of which benefit from an understanding of lower bounds on the entanglement needed to implement a given channel as an NLQC. However, the properties of a channel that lead to it having an entanglement cost in NLQC have remained unclear, with most lower bounds only applying to specially constructed examples. Here, we give a new lower bound technique for unitaries based on scrambling: we find that a unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble. Further, we find that the tripartite mutual information, an entropic object that quantifies the degree of scrambling, provides a quantitative lower bound on entanglement cost in NLQC. This is the first known lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries in NLQC which is faithful. Our results also relate scrambling and NLQC for the first time. Leveraging the faithful scrambling based bound, we then show that the controllable correlation, an earlier studied quantity, is also a faithful lower bound, resolving an earlier conjecture of Cleve and May.

articles.title: Look Mum, No Hands! Quantum State Preparation without Time-Dependent Control
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much can be prepared with a quantum system whose Hamiltonian cannot be modulated in time? Common intuition suggests that the answer is not much. Without a knob to turn during the evolution, a system seems confined to a fixed trajectory through its state space, while time-dependent control can steer it almost anywhere. We put this intuition to the test by studying autonomous control, i.e., state preparation with a time-invariant Hamiltonian, where the only freedom lies in the static coupling strengths and the evolution time. We characterize basic mathematical properties of the autonomously reachable set and introduce two criteria of unreachability: a certificate that is cheap to evaluate and rigorously excludes that a target state can be reached for any choice of control parameters, and a stronger criterion based on exhaustive numerical optimization. With these tools we estimate the probability that a typical state in Hilbert space is unreachable under randomly drawn control terms. The dimensionality of the reachable set turns out to be independent of the system, yet the fraction of Hilbert space lying close to it depends strongly on the choice of control Hamiltonians. Strikingly, for sufficiently random controls and long enough evolution times, almost every state can become approximately reachable, even with the fewest generators that permit full controllability with time-dependent couplings. Autonomous control can approach the expressivity of time-dependent control, at the cost of longer evolution times.

articles.title: Collective Superconducting-Qubit Interfaces for Microwave-to-Optical Quantum Transduction
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Mechanically mediated transducers, however, remain limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. In this work, we study a transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, we show that ensemble size and optical pump strength together set the conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation, the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, accelerating transfer of an excitation into the mechanics. We show that this speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so the single-qubit coupling and lifetime still set the coherence requirement. Transferring exactly one excitation also requires an anharmonic mechanical mode, which an auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics can provide. In a lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark with four qubits and $g_{\rm sm}/(2\pi)=3.81\,\mathrm{kHz}$, a mechanical anharmonicity of $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from $19.6\%$ to $99.7\%$. Finally, we quantify the effects of decoherence, disorder, residual qubit--qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise, finding that pair-dependent interactions reduce the optical retrieval efficiency from 58\% to 35\%. articles.title: Optimal Joint Bounds for Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation and Ground-State Preparation
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP) are fundamental problems in quantum computing. Given a Hamiltonian $H$ with $\|H\|\le1$ and a guiding state $|\psi\rangle$ with overlap at least $\gamma>0$ with the ground space of $H$, the goal in GSEE is to estimate the ground-state energy of $H$ to additive error $\delta$ with failure probability at most $\varepsilon$, while in GSP it is to prepare a state with ground-space weight at least $1-\varepsilon$, given a gap lower bound $\Delta$. Their costs are measured by quantum query complexity, i.e., the number of oracle calls needed to access $H$. Recent work proved optimal bounds $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ for GSEE and $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ for GSP in the time-evolution and block-encoding models. However, these models do not directly account for the sparsity of $H$, measured by the maximum number $s$ of nonzero entries in any row or column. In the sparse-access model, oracles instead return the locations and values of these entries. This introduces the additional parameter $s$, and it remained open how query complexity depends jointly on $s$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ or $\Delta$, and $\varepsilon$. We resolve this by proving sparse-query lower bounds $\Omega(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ for GSEE and $\Omega(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ for GSP, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. We also show that these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower-bound scalin

articles.title: Symmetry classification of hyperfine rovibrational molecular phase space
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetry-based structures have advanced molecular spectroscopy and quantum information science, yet connections between these fields remain largely unexplored. We construct a phase space theory of a molecule by jointly treating rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as the quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecule's point group. The various combinations of how these three degrees of freedom transform under symmetries organize a molecule's states into molecular species, and we show that each species is defined by a particular absolutely maximally entangled (AME) carrier state, or, for 45 species, by a two-dimensional space of them. Up to local unitaries and the order of the sectors, molecular species realize 21 AME states across 75 point groups: a product state, four maximally entangled pairs, and 16 genuinely tripartite states. A Fourier transform on the quotient relates orientation and angular-momentum descriptions while preserving these carrier states. We propose an example experimental protocol for preparing and driving symmetry-adapted bend states of $\mathrm{CaOCH_3}$.

articles.title: Qubit-qumode simulation of molecular torsion in photoisomerization
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photochemical reactions driven by large nuclear motion, such as the photoisomerization of retinal, depend strongly on both the global anharmonic forces of the potential and the periodic topology of molecular torsion. In this work, we develop a hybrid discrete (qubit) and continuous variable (qumode) quantum simulation framework for photochemical reactions that maps electronic states to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and the periodic torsion to a compact qumode encoding. Applying this approach to the two-mode Hahn-Stock and three-mode PSB3 models of retinal photoisomerization, we compare i) local vibronic approximations, ii) the full trigonometric potential on the noncompact line, and iii) the same potential on the compact circle, which matches the molecular torsion topology. We numerically show that the topological description can significantly alter relevant observables. We realize the compact torsion via both a wrapped Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoding and a two-qumode circle encoding and introduce two methods that reduce the hardware resources of both encodings. Spreading an encoded coordinate over several qumodes lowers the average occupation number of each mode, and adding counterterms to the Hamiltonian reduces the required squeezing amount. We expect that these methods make percent-level simulations of the considered molecules promising targets for hybrid qubit-qumode hardware. For more complex molecules, each additional nuclear coordinate is represented directly as a single qumode or an encoded register using th

articles.title: Experimental constraints on gauge hidden-variable models in Bell tests
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum mechanics assigns identical statistics to measurement procedures that realize the same final effect, irrespective of the transformations used to reach it. We test this operational equivalence with polarization-entangled photons by implementing one of Bob's analyzer settings either directly or through closed wave-plate trajectories $C_\gamma$ calibrated to produce the same measurement operator. Motivated by ontological descriptions in which a hidden frame is transported between contexts, we formulate a local path-memory model and derive the mixed-context bound $|S_\gamma^{\rm mix}|\leq 2+2p_\gamma$. The quantity $p_\gamma$ is a coupling-dependent counterfactual mismatch probability: it bounds a contextual Bell expression, but neither generates nor predicts the quantum Bell correlation. We therefore test path memory through the observable difference between direct and looped implementations, using a no-signaling phenomenological response in which a hidden holonomy $\delta_\gamma$ modifies one correlation term in $S_\gamma^{\rm mix}$. The direct reference violates the Bell inequality, while the looped mixed-context curves remain indistinguishable from it within the experimental precision. Our results support the quantum equivalence of calibrated measurement implementations and constrain path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions that predict an observable memory of the optical history.

articles.title: High-rate low-distance color codes
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experimental implementations of two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have surpassed the fidelity of physical qubits. A natural next step is to investigate higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits. Here we propose small, high-rate 2D color codes for this purpose. We design distance-$3$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/3$ and distance-$4$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/4$. We prove that these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic. We benchmark the codes by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity. The two best-performing codes have parameters $[[20,4,4]]$ and $[[16,4,4]]$ and achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of $0.22\%$ and $0.26\%$, respectively. These results match the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes that use weight-$5$ measurements.

articles.title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.

articles.title: Quantum Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport in spacetime through spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac distributions and spatiotemporal states
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport is a mathematical framework that determines the most efficient way to transform one probability distribution into another while minimizing a given cost function. Its central constructions include the Wasserstein distances, which quantify the space of probability distributions, and dual formulations that link to convex analysis. Its standard quantum generalization replaces probability distributions with density operators and cost function with positive semidefinite cost operator, which should be regarded as spatial quantum optimal transport. In this work, we propose the quantum optimal transport problem in spacetime through the spatiotemporal phase-space Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution and spatiotemporal states and through spatiotemporal state. We show that the two formalisms are equivalent and related via spatiotemporal operator frames. In the Kirkwood-Dirac phase-space formalism, the spatiotemporal distribution and the cost function are complex-valued, and the spatiotemporal couplings are Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions that yield the correct marginals for the local states. In the spatiotemporal state formalism, the cost operators are generally non-Hermitian, and the spatiotemporal couplings are generally non-Hermitian and yield the correct reduced local states. The Margenau-Hill phase-space distribution gives rise to a real-valued optimal transport in spatiotemporal phase space; in the spatiotemporal state formalism, this corresponds to a Hermitian spatiotemporal

articles.title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.

articles.title: Degree and normalization frontiers for bounded QSVT inversion
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) implements matrix inversion using bounded polynomials. Increasing polynomial degree can improve normalization and reduce amplified query cost, with savings that depend on the error criterion. However, existing bounded methods either fix the normalization or work far below the condition numbers of fault-tolerant resource estimates. We therefore analyze this trade-off for absolute reciprocal error, which controls inverse-operator accuracy, and for residual error, which suffices for normalized linear solves. For absolute reciprocal error, we establish a scaling limit to a constrained least-norm problem for entire functions and characterize its high-accuracy frontier using elliptic integrals. Constructions built from near-optimal limiting functions achieve certified query-cost savings over the rescaled minimax baseline of at least 11.8 percent at condition number ten thousand with error one millionth, and at least 22.8 percent at one million with error one ten-billionth. A simpler two-term rule also has certified savings, and its phase factors at condition number ten thousand pass numerical checks at selected points. For residual error, a sparse Chebyshev construction achieves certified savings over the residual-minimax baseline of at least 8.7 percent at condition number ten thousand with normalized-state error at most one hundred-millionth, and at least 13.1 percent at one million with error at most one ten-billionth. These results quantify the saving that a joint choice of degree and

articles.title: Quantum resources and the onset of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.

articles.title: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from

articles.title: Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite Qubit System
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

articles.title: Spectral Disks for Quantum Markov Generators
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral bounds for Markov generators require a choice of time scale. In quantum dynamics, a rate read off from a jump representation, the escape rate from a pure state and the smallest spectral disk need not agree. We prove that the spectrum of every GKLS generator written without a Hamiltonian lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis, with radius given by the norm of the operator $\Phi^\dagger(I)$ built from the jump map $\Phi$. This settles the first two scaling conjectures of "Corralling spectra of generators of time-continuous Markov evolution (both classical and quantum)", J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {59}, 175202 (2026). The third, escape-rate conjecture fails for a qutrit with a single normal jump. Nevertheless, twice the escape rate bounds every decay rate of any positive trace-preserving semigroup For GKLS generators with vanishing canonical Hamiltonian, four times the escape rate always supplies a spectral disk, and the factor four is optimal uniformly in dimension. We compare these bounds with classical Cassini ovals and thermodynamic ellipses, explain the obstacles to their quantum extensions, and formulate optimization over completely positive jump-map representations as a semidefinite program.

articles.title: Instrument indeterminacy: separating uncertainty in POVM effects and its neutrosophic reading
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple $(t,i,f)$ to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM $\{A, I-A\}$ we define the instrument indeterminacy $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A) = 4 \mathrm{Tr}(\rho(A-A^2))$, which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as $4TF = \mathcal{I}_\rho(A) + 4 \mathrm{Var}_\rho(A)$, a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A)$ from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to $m$-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A)$ equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated L\"uders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.

articles.title: Perspectives on the hidden subgroup problem over unitriangular groups
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP) over the upper unitriangular group $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$. While efficient quantum algorithms were discovered for some families of non abelian groups and nil-2 $p$-groups, no efficient algorithms are known for groups of nilpotency class higher than 2. The only techniques known for such groups scale exponentially in the size of the input. We first study the group $U_4(\mathbb{F}_p)$, the smallest upper unitriangular group exhibiting nilpotency class three. We analyze the application of the Pretty Good Measurement approach used for Heisenberg groups and show its limits. We then focus on the more general case $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$ to adapt existing techniques to this particular structure. In particular, we derive an algorithm for cyclic subgroups as a subroutine for a general algorithm, although it is not efficient in the size of the group. Our results highlight the difficulties introduced by the increasing nilpotency class and suggests some directions for an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP over $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$.

articles.title: Uniformly Convergent Perturbation Theory for Open Quantum Systems at, near, and away from Exceptional Points
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.23604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Near a Liouvillian exceptional point, spectral perturbation theory becomes ill-conditioned, yet the observable dynamics of a finite-dimensional open system remains regular in the perturbation. Using a Dyson expansion, which requires no diagonalization of the perturbed generator, we analyze the scaling, stability, and convergence of the perturbative corrections at, near and away from exceptional points. We derive scaling laws showing that nonperipheral Jordan blocks raise the degree of the polynomial-in-time factors multiplying decaying exponentials, which are present for any generator as resonances, and we quantify this excess. We further establish a uniform-in-time error estimate for the perturbative series, valid for any relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladian and controlled by a parameter $q = |\varepsilon|R$, where $\varepsilon$ is the perturbation strength and $R$ is a constant built from unperturbed data. All constants of the bound remain continuous through an exceptional point when the coalescing eigenvalues are kept in one spectral cluster. The estimate extends to the frequency domain via the Laplace transform, and to time-dependent perturbations. We test it in a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point, including perturbations that break its symmetry.

articles.title: Decreased astrocytic CCL5 by Mir324 ameliorates ischemic stroke injury via the CCR5/ERK/CREB pathway
articles.summary: Following ischemic stroke, Ccl5 mRNA expression increased, while Mir324 expression decreased in the peri-infarct cortex of middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) mice. However, the roles of CCL5 and Mir324 in stroke remained largely unclear. Here, we show that inhibiting CCL5 using antibodies or Mir324 not only reduced infarct area and preserved neurological function in MCAO mice but also attenuated astrocyte reactivity and microglial activation, protected dendritic structures, and maintained spine density. In an astrocyte-neuron co-culture system after oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD), inhibiting astrocytic CCL5 by antibody or Mir324 decreased neuronal apoptosis and preserved dendritic structure. Importantly, the suppression of CCL5 enhanced ERK/CREB pathway signaling both in vivo and in vitro. Consistent with these findings, the application of Maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist, reduced infarct size, decreased neuronal apoptosis, and upregulated the ERK/CREB pathway in neurons treated with OGD. In conclusion, targeting the CCL5 pathway via Mir324 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for alleviating ischemic stroke damage through modulation of the neuronal CCR5/ERK/CREB pathway.

articles.title: Explainable machine learning-assisted exploration of chromatin dynamics reveals chromosome-specific response to serum starvation
articles.summary: Chromatin is dynamic at all length scales, influencing chromatin-based processes, such as gene expression. Even large-scale reorganization of whole chromosome territories has been reported upon specific signals, but the lack of suitable methods has prevented analysis of the underlying dynamic processes. Here, we have used CRISPR-Sirius for time-lapse imaging of chromatin loci dynamics during serum starvation. We show that chromosome 1 loci move toward the nuclear envelope during the first hour of serum starvation in a chromosome-specific manner. Machine learning-assisted exploration of acquired multiparametric data combined with the Shapley values-based explanation approach allowed us to uncover the critical features that characterize chromatin dynamics during serum starvation. This analysis reveals that although serum starvation affects overall nuclear morphology and chromatin dynamics, chromosome 1 loci display a specific response that is characterized by maintenance of dynamics in a constrained environment, and long ‘jumps’ at the nuclear periphery. Interestingly, the two homologous chromosomes display differential behaviors, with the more peripheral homolog being more responsive to the signal than the internal one. Overall, the presented machine learning-assisted dataset exploration helps us navigate the multidimensional data to understand the underlying dynamic processes and can be applied to a wide variety of research questions in imaging and cell biology in general.

articles.title: Junctional and actomyosin dynamics drive endothelial cell rearrangements during vascular tube formation
articles.summary: Lumen formation is a key process during the morphogenesis of tubular organs, such as the vertebrate vascular network. At the cellular level, lumen formation can be achieved by cell shape changes or cell rearrangements. We have previously shown that such cell rearrangements are driven by oscillating membrane protrusions, called junction-based lamellipodia (JBL), which provide a ratchet mechanism driving convergent cell movements to connect local lumens, and generate vascular patency. By performing in vivo time-lapse imaging at high spatiotemporal resolution in zebrafish embryos, we have analyzed the cytoskeletal and junctional dynamics, which underlie JBL formation and function. We show that JBL formation requires the activity of the F-actin nucleation complex Arp2/3. We further show that a novel junction is formed at the distal end of the JBL from a pool of VE-cadherin originating from outside the initial JBL area. Subsequently, proximal and distal junctions merge and fuse, a process driven by actomyosin contractility. Prior to this fusion, we observe a specific recruitment of Myl9 within the interjunctional space. Furthermore, inhibition of actomyosin contractility abrogates junctional merging. Taken together, our analyses demonstrate that JBL constitute a module, which, by alternate generation of pushing forces (JBL formation) and pulling forces (junctional merging), provide the physical means for endothelial cells to elongate and to rearrange and thereby generate a continuous vascular lumen.

articles.title: Winding-up of fibrin fibers as a novel mechanism of platelet-mediated fiber compaction
articles.summary: This study reveals an unrecognized mechanism by which platelets retract and compact fibrin fibers. Using a newly developed 2D fiber-retraction assay, we observed a ‘gearwheel’ pattern of actomyosin in spread platelets with associated, extracellular fibrin patches that appear to initiate fibrin fiber attachment and rearrangement. The outcome of this process results in two morphologically different platelet populations. Spread platelets with coiled fibers around and above their pseudo-nucleus. Other, only partially spread platelets have tightly packed fibers around bulbous protrusions (‘bulbs’), mirroring the architecture of platelets and adjacent fibers within a retracted clot. Thus, the observed compaction process might take place during clot retraction to reduce clot volume, stiffen the clot, and enhance wound repair. Apart from pulling on fibers like on a rope, platelets actively wrap them into compact structures, similar to balls of wool. Using a combination of 3D clot- and 2D fiber-retraction assays, expansion and electron microscopy, live imaging, and mathematical modeling, we show that platelets use an actomyosin-driven motion to loop fibrin fibers around the base of bulbs, which form when platelets get trapped between fibrin fibers during 3D clot- or 2D fiber-retraction assays. These findings complement existing models of platel-mediated fibrin retraction, offering new insight into how platelets mechanically organize fibrin fibers.

articles.title: Rethinking laboratory sustainability
articles.summary: Green lab initiatives like My Green Lab and LEAF (Laboratory Efficiency Assessment Framework), are paving the way towards sustainable research by promoting resource efficiency, energy conservation, and waste reduction through behavioral changes. However, these initiatives focus almost exclusively on material consumption, overlooking deeper facets of scientific waste that stem from questionable research practices: the environmental cost of unnecessary or poorly designed experiments, discarded null results, unreproducible research, and distorted reporting. I argue that a more meaningful discussion of scientific sustainability must look beyond physical resource management to examine the scientific process itself; to rethink the questions we ask, the experiments we do, and how we communicate our findings. To build a truly sustainable scientific ecosystem, Green Lab initiatives must join forces with Open Science and research integrity movements to update not only the hardware, but also the software of science.

articles.title: Diurnal rhythmicity in metabolism and salivary effector expression shapes aphid performance on host plants
articles.summary: Diurnal rhythms influence insect behavior, physiology, and metabolism, optimizing their performance by adapting to daily changes in the environment. While their impact on agricultural pests has been briefly explored, our understanding of how these rhythms drive adaptive responses in pest biology and influence host colonization remains elusive. Here, we show that a notorious global aphid pest, Rhopalosiphum padi, exhibits distinct diurnal patterns in feeding behavior, with elevated honeydew excretion at night and extended phloem salivation during early nighttime. Temporal aphid transcriptome profiling reveals four diurnally rhythmic clusters, two of which peak at night, exhibiting enrichment in carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. Beyond the established role in manipulating host responses and allowing sustained feeding, our study reveals novel evidence of cyclical fluctuations in salivary effector expression in an insect species. Silencing key effector genes, peaking in expression during the increased nighttime salivation, results in a more pronounced reduction in aphid excretion activity on host plants during the night compared to the day, a phenomenon not observed on artificial diets. A better understanding of aphid diurnal rhythms and their roles in shaping aphid performance provides a promising avenue to refine and optimize pest management, granting a strategic advantage for minimizing crop damage.
